トリコロール 青の愛

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

解説・あらすじ

ポーランドの巨匠クシシュトフ・キエシロフスキ監督による、青、白、赤のフランス国旗をモチーフにした三部作「トリコロール」の第1作。 自動車事故で最愛の夫と娘を失ったジュリーは、すべてを引き払いパリでの生活を始める。静かな日々を過ごすジュリーは、音楽家であった亡き夫に愛人がいたことを知る。 ジュリーを演じるのは、「イングリッシュ・ペイシェント」「ショコラ」のジュリエット・ビノシュ。

article_text:
World premiering in competition at Cannes this year, where Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne jointly won the Best Actor prize, Lukas Dhont’s Coward has since been selected as Belgium’s Oscar entry. Ahead of a theatrical release from MUBI beginning on December 25, the first trailer has now arrived.

Here’s the synopsis: “Pierre (Macchia) arrives at the front lines as a young soldier eager to find his footing in a world consumed by violence. Everything changes when he meets Francis (Campagne), a kindred spirit whose vision of staging a front-line theatre show unlocks a world Pierre never knew existed. What begins as a fleeting escape from the harsh reality of the trenches soon blossoms into a tender, emotional love story, anchored by the undeniable chemistry of breakout actors Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne. As the world burns around them, their stage becomes a sanctuary of innocence and devotion.”

Savina Petkova said in her Cannes review, “Cinema has taken viewers to the trenches of World War I so often that audiences might as well have formed sensory memories of a throat-clenching terror, the screams drowned by a sudden explosion and ears ringing. It’s all artificial, of course, but film’s empathy machine is perfectly suited for such participatory experiences from the safety of our seats. Yet war, like love, has too many faces and facets to ever be extensively represented. Luckily for us, Flemish director Lukas Dhont has chosen exactly that setting for his third feature (after Girl and Close ) and first love story. Coward is one of those provocative titles called into question by everyone but the film’s protagonist. In the Belgian army (on the French side), Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia) and his mates take pleasure in naming others cowards, be it enemies or deserters, summarizing a hero/weakling binary from the get-go.”

article_text:
泉屋博古館東京（東京都港区）で、「唐物誕生――茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる」が11月3日から開催されます。

茶の湯デザインの3000年史――中世日本では、大陸との交流のなかで喫茶の風習がもたらされ、やがて「茶の湯」として独自の伝統文化を形成していきます。喫茶に用いられ、そして喫茶の場を彩る道具には「唐物」とよばれる大陸の文物が珍重され、当時の人々の価値観や美意識による選別を経て、いわゆる「名物」として評価されるものも登場しました。

本展ではこうした「唐物」が誕生する過程に焦点が当てられます。はるか中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介され、胡銅（古銅）とよばれる花入を切り口として、金工品や陶磁器、漆工など、素材を越えた共通性にも着目しながら、茶の湯デザインを東アジア文化史のなかに再定位することが試みられます。さらに、これまで未解明であった胡銅の鋳造技術にせまる特集コーナーも設け、最新の研究成果もあわせて紹介されます。

唐物誕生―茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる

会場：泉屋博古館東京（東京都港区六本木1-5-1）

会期：2026年11月3日（火・祝）～12月13日（日） 【前期：11/3～23 後期：11/25～12/13】

開館時間：11:00～18:00（金曜日は19:00まで） ※入館は閉館の30分前まで

休館日：月曜日（11/23は開館）、11/24

観覧料：一般1,500円、学生800円 ※学生ならびに18歳以下の方は証明書の提示が必要 ※障がい者手帳ご提示の方はご本人および同伴者1名まで無料

アクセス： 東京メトロ南北線「六本木一丁目」駅下車、北改札正面出口より屋外エスカレーターで3分 東京メトロ日比谷線「神谷町」駅下車、4b出口より徒歩10分 東京メトロ銀座線「溜池山王」駅下車、13番出口より徒歩10分

詳細は、 泉屋博古館東京公式サイト まで。

唐物とは

古代・中世において中国などから輸入された諸物貨に冠せられた和訓の総称（『国史大辞典』）。なかでも日中貿易が盛んになった鎌倉～室町時代には、さまざまな種類の「唐物」がもたらされ、それらはやがて成立してくる茶の湯のなかで貴重な茶道具として珍重されるようになりました。ただし、当時「唐物」と認識されていた文物はかならずしも中国産にはかぎられず、朝鮮半島や東南アジアで制作されたものや、あるいは国産品も含まれます。

本展では中世後期の日本で珍重された舶来の茶道具類を広く「唐物」とよび、中国文物を範としつつ、模倣やアレンジを加えて裾野が広がっていく茶の湯デザインの文化史的背景を、約三千年前の中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介することが試みられます。

展覧会構成

I いにしえへのあこがれ

いまから約三千年前、殷周時代に盛んにつくられた青銅器は、その造形レベルの高さからのちの時代の美術工芸の模範とされましたが、それだけでなく、周の時代は儒教のなかで理想の治世がなされた時代とされ、その遺風を伝える青銅器は特別に尊ばれるようになりました。「東洋のルネサンス」とも称される宋代では、こうした青銅器に対する関心が急速に高まり、同時代の陶磁器や金工品などのデザインにも強く影響をおよぼすようになります。本章では住友コレクションのほこる中国古代青銅器と、いにしえへのあこがれから生み出された工芸品をともに展示し、のちの「唐物」へと受け継がれるデザインの源流が紹介されます。

II 規範の形成 宋元時代の喫茶文化と文物

宋代以降、士大夫と呼ばれる知識人層が当時の政治・文化の中心をになうようになり、彼らの価値観が強く反映された文物が重視されるようになります。同時に、点茶法とよばれる喫茶も流行し、その用途にかなう道具や、喫茶の空間を飾る工芸品も生み出されました。やがて、こうした文物にあらわされたデザインは、のちの時代まで受け継がれる「規範」を形成し、東アジアの文化に多大な影響を与えるようになります。本章では中国宋元時代の絵画・工芸作品を一堂に会し、この時代の中国で生み出された「古典」とはいかなるものかを探っていきます。

III 日中交易と喫茶文化の伝来

日本中世では、海上交易を通じて大陸との交流が活発におこなわれ、当時の最先端の流行であった喫茶文化にかかわる文物ももたらされることとなりました。それらが日本国内で特に珍重されるようになり、やがて「唐物」として茶の湯の形成に大きな役割を果たします。一方で、単に中国文化に追随するだけでなく、国内でそれを模したもの、そこから日本独自のデザインへと進化したものも生み出されています。本章では日本と大陸の交流の証、そしてメイドインジャパンの胎動を示す作品から、喫茶の受容と文化交流のあり方にせまっていきます。

IV 『君台観左右帳記』の時代

日本にもたらされた大陸の文物は、時の権力者によっても重視されるようになり、彼らによって活発にコレクションされるようになります。なかでも足利幕府八代将軍の足利義政が所蔵したとされる「東山御物」と、その飾り方や鑑定に関する指南書である『君台観左右帳記』は、のちの時代の茶の湯のあり方に大きな影響を与えました。そこでは単に中国文化を受容するだけでなく、当時の日本人の価値観による選別のプロセスが働いており、「唐物」というカテゴリーがまさに日本文化現象としてかたちづくられたことが、当時の作品群から見えてきます。本章ではそうした様相を、いわゆる「東山御物」の名品たちを中心に見ることができます。

V そして利休へ

当初は中国文化の強い影響下で形成された喫茶文化は、中世後期になると、徐々に日本独自のものへと変貌を遂げていきます。喫茶の空間を飾る道具たちも、いわゆる「唐物」のみならず、国産の道具が評価を上げていくことになります。「和漢のさかいをまぎらかす」ことが重視されていくわけですが、そうしたなか登場する千利休が、いわゆる「わび茶」の大成者として歴史的に評価されていくことになります。しかし、利休の時代に用いられていた道具を見ていくと、意外にも大陸的要素の強いものがすくなくないことに気づきます。そして、そのなかには中国古代青銅器からの系譜を連綿と受け継ぐデザインも見られるのです。本章では、利休のめざした茶の湯のあり方と、そこに受け継がれる中国古代からの系譜を、名品たちのなかから探っていきます。

特集展示 胡銅の鋳造技術をさぐる

茶の湯の世界ではもっとも格式の高い、真の花入として重視される胡銅。中国古代青銅器を模したデザインが見られることから、「唐物」としてあつかわれることの多い胡銅ですが、実はその産地については未解明の点が多くのこされています。謎多き胡銅の実態解明をめざして、泉屋博古館は茶道資料館・芦屋釜の里とともに胡銅の鋳造技術の調査を進め、その成果にもとづいて胡銅桃尻花入の鋳造実験にも取り組んできました。この特集展示では実験の成果を公開し、胡銅という「唐物」が誕生する過程について、鋳造技術という観点からせまっていきます。

絵画・陶磁器・漆工品・金工品など幅広いジャンルから、国宝6点、重要文化財9点を含む約80点が出品（前後期の展示替えあり）される本展。泉屋博古館と茶道資料館（裏千家・今日庵）、芦屋釜の里の三者が結集して、茶の湯デザインの源流に迫っていきます。教科書にも登場する国宝や重要文化財の息をのむ美しさを間近で体感できるだけでなく、最新の鋳造実験によって胡銅の謎に迫るなど、非常に挑戦的な内容となっており、茶の湯ファンはもちろん、東洋美術や工芸愛好家にも見逃せない機会となるはずです。およそ3000年にわたる壮大なデザインの変遷をたどりながら、茶の湯文化の源流をさぐる意欲的な展示を、ぜひ会場で堪能してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
L’impatto personale con la mostra di Giovanni Kronenberg negli spazi della galleria di Sara Zanin a Roma, visitabile fino al 31 ottobre, mi ha lasciato una sensazione precisa: per entrare davvero in sintonia con il suo lavoro occorre accogliere un invito allo smarrimento. Camminare tra le sue opere significa accettare che l’arte non debba spiegare, descrivere o condurre lungo un itinerario preordinato, piuttosto abitare il mistero, la sospensione e una essenziale ambiguità.

È a partire da questa esperienza visiva che è nato un lungo dialogo con l’artista: una conversazione a ruota libera che, più che focalizzarsi sui singoli lavori esposti ha toccato i nodi centrali della sua pratica, del suo rapporto con la materia, con il tempo e con i valori sottesi al suo gesto artistico.

In Kronenberg l’opera si offre sempre come forma di interrogazione aperta che chiede silenzio. Questa attitudine nasce da un rapporto intimo e stratificato con il suo collezionismo. Punto di partenza del suo lavoro è spesso l’incontro casuale con oggetti che lo seducono: reperti semplicemente trovati o segnalati da rigattieri di fiducia che ne conoscono la sensibilità.

L’acquisto non risponde mai a una progettazione preliminare o a una motivazione razionale; il “non capire” rappresenta per l’artista il presupposto fondamentale e il nutriente per l’innesco del processo creativo. Depositati negli spazi della sua casa – ormai trasformata in una sorta di “opera totale” – questi oggetti riposano e sedimentano anche per lunghi periodi. Poi, improvvisamente e senza un motivo apparente, scatta una riaffascinazione, una scintilla che scaturisce dalla complessità linguistica che si crea in rapporto ad altri oggetti.

In questo processo le cose e i linguaggi si trasformano nel tempo accompagnandosi a quel cambiamento sociale di cui noi stessi siamo parte. Così la memoria storica intrinseca all’oggetto si intreccia indissolubilmente con la memoria personale.

È il caso, ad esempio, del manichino presente in mostra, riletto e riconfigurato attraverso l’incontro con materiali diversi che hanno generato una nuova osmosi tra le parti. Talvolta è proprio la contrapposizione temporale e funzionale degli elementi accostati a determinare una misteriosa carica drammatica. In fondo, per Kronenberg fare arte significa letteralmente “fare cose che non si sanno”, avventurandosi in territori inesplorati senza il bisogno stringente di dover fornire risposte.

Questa libertà si riflette anche nella sua posizione rispetto alla permanenza/ stabilità dei materiali. Kronemberg accetta e include la volatile mutabilità della materia, collegandola alla mobilità stessa dei significati. Si dichiara interessato al “qui e ora” linguistico, al momento esatto di questa cristallizzazione, senza preoccuparsi del destino futuro degli elementi più effimeri (come l’odore impregnato su una spugna, destinato inevitabilmente a svanire nel tempo).

Quando le opere entrano nello spazio espositivo, l’atto dell’installare assume una valenza rituale e spirituale. L’arte, per Kronenberg, parla da sempre della diade fondamentale vita/morte e conserva per questo una tensione intrinsecamente drammatica. Per enfatizzarla, l’artista procede per sottrazione e isolamento trattando le opere quasi come icone religiose: l’isolamento dell’oggetto ne potenzia l’aura, mentre la regia dello spazio si focalizza sul dettaglio spiazzante anziché sull’accumulazione.

Parallelamente alla pratica scultorea il disegno si sviluppa come presenza galleggiante, apparizione che si pone in un rapporto di osmosi con le forme tridimensionali. Mai cavalcata la tecnica del monocromo – ritenuta dall’artista troppo “facile” sul piano linguistico – le recenti sperimentazioni vedono l’impiego di fondi in metallo ossidato, fogli di rame e palladio (in sostituzione dell’oro per far galleggiare maggiormente le forme) che accentuano questa spinta verso un’idea di religiosità laica, carica di pathos.

Il disegno nasce come un piacere puro, come avanzamento intuitivo senza alcuna griglia progettuale. Disegnare, per Kronenberg, è «Come nuotare al largo senza sapere dove si arriverà», un gesto che spinge verso l’alterità e contribuisce ad amplificare la complessità dell’approccio con lo spazio.

In questo percorso, l’artista si colloca innanzitutto come il primo spettatore delle proprie opere. Sottraendosi alla tentazione di spiegare o categorizzare la sua ricerca dentro i soliti cliché, lascia chi osserva completamente libero di attivare le proprie personali associazioni. Nella sua arte non c’è compiacimento né ambizione descrittiva: c’è solo la consapevolezza che il “non capire” sia una dimensione dialettica preziosa e che, per incontrare davvero un’opera, sia indispensabile concedersi la libertà di perdersi.

article_text:
Paris Jackson is claiming the executor of her father’s fortune and legacy, has once again failed “to meet his fundamental disclosure obligations” despite a very explicit court order on those money matters. At the same time, Jackson says John Branca wants to hand out tens of millions to himself and his law firm.

Calling the assertions and the demands for financial consequences “nonsensical” in response, the flush Michael Jackson Estate once again wants the deceased superstar’s daughter to beat it, to put it politely.

With a December 4 hearing penciled in with retired Judge Mitchell Beckloff for this latest dust-up between the ‘Zombies in Love’ singer and the Michael EP, Paris Jackson’s team view things in very black and white terms.

Universal Becomes First Studio To Pass $5 Billion At Year-To-Date Global Box Office

“Enough of the smoke and mirrors — Paris is asking to reduce the management fee,” a spokesperson for the younger Jackson told Deadline. “Executor Branca has repeatedly failed to meet deadlines ordered by the judge that are in place to provide Paris and her siblings visibility about how the Estate is being run. Since money is what motivates Executor Branca, this is the only way to enforce the timeline he agreed to.”

Watch on Deadline

To be precise , in a filing in LA Superior Court late last week, Paris Jackson’s Stradling Yocca Carlson & Rauth attorneys accuse longtime foe Branca of playing loose with the rules that he himself insisted upon.

“Executor has violated the Court’s April 24, 2026 order by failing to meet his own self-selected, and then extended, deadline,” states the 12-page motion. “Despite having years to prepare these already belated accountings, Executor quietly filed incomplete documents styled as putative accounts current for 2023 and 2024. The 2023 filing expressly notes the material ways in which it is incomplete. As for 2024, it is nothing more than a placeholder. Neither of these defective filings provides a basis on which the Court could give its approval. Executor, however, neither sought relief from the Court nor committed to filing complete and accurate 2023 or 2024 accountings on any particular date.”

The filing is full of citations of alleged past violations of disclosures and obligations in what has become a very public and dragged out conflict between Michael Jackson and Debbie Rowe’s second child and the controversial Thriller superstar’s on-again/off-again lawyer.

However, one figure in this latest document stands out.

“This instance, however, is particularly offensive in that Executor’s defective filings include a request for approval of more than one hundred million dollars ($100,000,000) in compensation for the co-executors and the Ziffren firm,” the October 23 motion says. To rub that in, the document adds with barely veiled sarcasm: “It is unclear how Executor could calculate and distribute such an amount with any confidence and yet be unable to file complete and accurate accountings years later.”

Put in that context, and with the history between the parties (blockbuster biopic and all), “difficult” may be the kindest term one could use.

The motion from Paris Jackson goes on to declare: “Paris therefore requests that the Court reduce the compensation to Co-Executors for 2023, 2024 and each consecutive year until such time as Executor files a complete and accurate 2026 account current, by five percentage points, i.e. , from 15% to 10% of the gross entertainment-related income.”

While 28-year-old Paris Jackson has reportedly received about $65 million from her late father’s now multi-billion dollar estate, which was over $500 million in debt at the time of MJ’s 2009 prescription drug OD death, she has been demanding a deeper dive into the books from Branca and now dead co-executor John McClain for a while. Claiming sweetheart deals, bonuses and payouts for no or little work, legal fees, and swaths of unnecessary expenses (like the tens of millions in reshoots for a near completed Antoine Fuqua -directed Michael after the unearthing of a very restrictive 1994 deal — along with a $20 million-plus settlement — with the family of then-underaged Jordan Chandler), Paris has had some wins and losses in what is pretty obviously a long term goal of taking control of the estate itself.

Or not, according to the MJ Estate itself today.

“It is an understatement to say that this motion is completely without merit, nor is it argued on facts, the estate’s spokesperson told Deadline Wednesday. “Plaintiff’s attorneys have motioned for a reduction in executor compensation, when in fact the executors waived that from the estate’s beginning, and have never taken any executor compensation. They are paid a separate, court-ordered management fee for operating the hugely successful Michael Jackson business.”

Not mentioning that $100 million, Team Branca add: “It is also nonsensical that the motion seeks absurd penalties for the 2023 and 2024 accountings which have already been filed or for the 2025 and 2026 accountings which are not required to be filed for another six and 14 months, respectively.”

BTW – whatever goes down on December 4, with a sequel to the $1.02 billon and more box office busting Michael in the works , don’t for one second think this de facto Jackson civil war is anywhere near over.

article_text:
Archives – November 2, 2023

This year, the major exhibition on the beach in Deauville brings together two photographers who never met – Robert Doisneau, who died on 1 April 1994 , and Malick Sidibé, who came to Paris for the first time in January 1995 – the two of them could have been great friends!

On the one hand, Robert Doisneau, probably the most popular and best-loved French photographer, known for his famous photos taken in post-war Paris, for the tenderness and gentle irony shining through his pictures, which are part of an immense body of work, made up of history and humanity. On the other, Malick Sidibé, famous in Bamako and all the region since the 1960s, who combined studio portraits and festivities, leaving us hundreds of thousands of photos, now well-known all over the world. A portait of Africa by itself, both tender and amusing, of great value both from a historic and a human perspective.

The dialogue between two worlds and two cultures is illustrated by the choice of series exhibited, which are not well known: Palm Springs, (in colour!) from a photo-reportage made by Doisneau in 1960, on the construction of golf courses in Palm Springs, a refuge for rich American pensioners, and the pictures, many hitherto unseen, of Bamako youth, photographed by Sidibé in the early 1970s, at the town’s brand-new swimming pool or on the banks of the River Niger.

"ES：我知道你的许多摄影作品都集中在记录墨西哥移民和无证移民社群。在当前政府的领导下，对于这个社群来说，这是一个充满挑战且令人恐慌的时期。在过去的一年里，你的创作过程改变了吗？LMT：我的创作过程发生了显著的变化，这种变化源于我对所拍摄之人的责任感。自1995年以来，我的许多作品都围绕着墨西哥移民和无证移民社群展开，通常是通过与家庭、身份、移民、记忆和归属感相关的亲密影像。多年来，拍摄真人一直是我接近这些主题方式的核心。最近，对于制作或公开分享可辨认个人身份的照片，我变得越来越犹豫。这些照片中的人不是抽象概念或符号；他们是信任我的人。此时此刻，我不希望我的创作或展览行为给任何人带来额外的恐惧或曝光风险。这种担忧改变了我的拍摄对象以及我对可见性的思考方式。因此，我开始转向更具诗意和间接性的影像。这些作品仍然取材于墨西哥文化、个人历史、家庭以及塑造了我的视觉语言，但我现在对制作依赖于可辨认人物的照片兴趣不大了。在某些方面，恐惧迫使作品形式发生了转变。我在探讨：当面孔无法出现时，缺席、物体、风景、手势、象征主义和文化记忆如何能够承载一个故事。我尚不知道这会通往何方，但这种不确定性让我觉得很重要。", Photography Educator: Lupita Murillo Tinnen

©Lupita Murillo Tinnen, Petronila, Domestic Worker, arrived at age 23, Matamoros, Puebla

Photography Educator is a monthly series on Lenscratch that highlights outstanding photography teachers who inspire students of all ages. Each month, the series celebrates an educator’s insights, strategies, and excellence in fostering creativity and resilience.

It gives me great pleasure to feature Lupita Murillo Tinnen this month, not only as an insightful artist but also as a gifted educator and mentor. Her commitment to supporting photographers and fellow teachers reflects a belief in the importance of cultivating creative voices. As Lupita puts it, “the most meaningful part of my job is helping faculty succeed so that they, in turn, can help students succeed”. That same care for others resonates in her own photographic work, which I deeply admire for its ability to bring personal stories into broader conversations about labor and identity. Informed by her own experience as a first-generation Mexican American, her photographs ask us to consider whose stories are told and whose experiences remain overlooked.

This article includes a selection of Lupita’s documentary portraits of Mexican immigrants, an interview, images and statements from some of her students.

©Lupita Murillo Tinnen, Rene, Construction, arrived at age 25, Guanajuato

©Lupita Murillo Tinnen, Carlos, Maintenance, arrived at age 19, Guanajuato

©Lupita Murillo Tinnen, Angelica, Building Cleaning Worker, Queretaro

Social documentary photography has been an extension of my professional life for nearly thirty years. Throughout my photographic career, the subject of my work has been the Mexican immigrant and undocumented community.

In the spirit of Richard Avedon, August Sander, Irving Penn, and more recently, Peter Yang, my contribution includes a photographic record of immigrant laborers currently residing in North Texas who are from Latin American countries. Unlike Avedon who was an outsider from New York, I have a unique perspective as an insider who comes from a working-class family of Mexican immigrants. I compare my work to the archives of German documentary photographer, August Sander, who catalogued social types in the period between the two World Wars. Sander’s goal was to create a major archive documenting the diverse social characteristics of German people. I have created a documentary record of the many hardworking immigrant laborers who usually are relegated to the status of ‘non-belonging other’ and not as an equal. Instead of marginalizing the laborer by depicting them in their work environment, or in a uniform, they are dressed in their chosen attire and collaborate in the decisions regarding their portrayal. My aim is to expose the laborers as more than a simple statistic; instead, there is a face for the viewer to meet and encounter as an equal due in part to the large size of the prints. This body of work challenges social realist depictions of immigrant laborers, historically created by rhetoric, that produce the immigrant laborer as merely a worker rather than as an individual with a story. I combine text, graphics, and historical images of workers to create narratives concerning the individuals portrayed. These allow the viewer an opportunity to spend more time with each image. In contrast to the dominant tradition of stark realism long associated with social documentary photography, the photographs in this project are digital collages constructed onto large 30”x40” or 20”x24”white backgrounds.

ES: For a little background, can you share how you got into photography, teaching, and your present position as Dean of Academic Affairs and Workforce? Did you always want to work in academia? LMT: My relationship with photography began when I was nine years old and desperately wanted a hot pink 110 film camera for Christmas. Once I had it, I photographed everything. I made little still lifes and regularly recruited my younger sister to be my model. It was playful, but even then I was interested in arranging the world within a frame. Photography became something more serious when I took a class in high school. That experience changed the course of my life. My teacher, Terry Buckner, encouraged me to consider college and to study photography, which was not a path I had imagined for myself. Coming from a family of Mexican immigrants, I did not grow up knowing that going to college was something I could do. I did not initially set out to build a career in academia. I discovered that calling in graduate school at the University of North Texas, where I became a graduate assistant under Dornith Doherty. I loved the classroom, and I especially loved introducing students to the magic of the darkroom: watching an image emerge in the developer and seeing students realize that they could make something entirely their own. I knew then that I wanted to teach. After approximately 17 years in the classroom, I decided to apply for an associate dean position. I discovered that I also loved the work that happens behind the scenes in higher education. I am highly organized, I genuinely do not mind paperwork, and I enjoy solving problems and creating the conditions that allow other people to do their best work. Today, as Dean of Academic Affairs and Workforce, my impact is less visible than it was in the classroom, but it is broader. I may not teach students directly anymore, but I can support the faculty, programs, and systems that shape their education. I have found another way to teach and serve.

ES: Did you have an influential photography mentor or teacher? What was their biggest impact on you as both an artist and an educator? LMT: I have been extraordinarily fortunate to have several teachers and mentors who changed the trajectory of my life, often by seeing possibilities for me before I could see them for myself. My high school photography teacher, Terry Buckner, was the first person who told me that I could go to college and study photography. That simple encouragement was transformative. She gave me permission to imagine a future I did not yet know existed. In college, Stan Godwin took a chance on me and hired me to work in the photography area as a student worker. That experience gave me a sense of belonging in the department and allowed me to begin seeing photography not simply as something I studied, but as a community in which I could contribute. Bill McDowell encouraged me to pursue graduate school and, importantly, encouraged me to continue photographing my family. He helped me understand that the people, experiences, and cultural history closest to me were worthy subjects for serious artistic inquiry. He also introduced me to Dornith Doherty, who became enormously influential in the development and direction of my work at the University of North Texas. Later, my Ph.D. chair, Marilyn Waligore, helped me bring together my creative practice and scholarly thinking. Each of these mentors gave me something different, but collectively they taught me one of the most important lessons I carried into teaching and now into administration: educators can alter a student’s sense of what is possible. Sometimes a student needs instruction. Sometimes they need critique. And sometimes they simply need someone they respect to say, “You can do this.”

ES: I know that much of your photography has concentrated on documenting the Mexican immigrant and undocumented community. These are very challenging and frightful times for this community with the current administration. Has your process changed in the last year? LMT: My process has changed significantly, and the change has come from a sense of responsibility toward the people I photograph. Since 1995, much of my work has centered on Mexican immigrant and undocumented communities, often through intimate images connected to family, identity, migration, memory, and belonging. For many years, photographing real people was essential to how I approached those subjects. More recently, I have become increasingly hesitant to make or publicly share photographs in which individuals could be identified. The people in these photographs are not abstractions or symbols; they are human beings who have trusted me. At this moment, I do not want the act of making or exhibiting my work to create additional fear or exposure for anyone. That concern has changed both what I photograph and how I think about visibility. As a result, I have begun moving toward more poetic and indirect imagery. The work still draws from Mexican culture, personal history, family, and the visual language that has shaped me, but I am less interested right now in making a photograph that depends on an identifiable person. In some ways, fear has forced a formal shift in the work. I am asking how absence, objects, landscape, gesture, symbolism, and cultural memory can carry a story when a face cannot. I do not yet know where that will lead, but that uncertainty feels important.

ES: What are some of the challenges you see for educators in the arts at this moment in time? What challenges do your students face? LMT: One of the most significant challenges for arts educators right now is undoubtedly artificial intelligence, but I also see it as an extraordinary creative opportunity. Photography has always been shaped by technological disruption. I began in the darkroom and lived through the transition to digital photography, the rise of camera phones, and the moment when many people wondered whether ubiquitous cameras would diminish the role of the photographer. They did not. In much the same way that photography did not eliminate painting, new technologies tend to change creative practice rather than end it. They force us to reconsider authorship, process, craft, and what makes an image matter. I have therefore tried to approach AI with curiosity rather than fear. Creative people will experiment with it, resist it, misuse it, critique it, and eventually invent new forms and movements because of it. The challenge for educators is helping students participate in that experimentation without surrendering the learning itself. That is where I think students are particularly vulnerable. Students do not always know what they do not yet know. If they routinely offload the difficult parts of thinking, writing, problem-solving, or making to AI before they have developed those abilities themselves, they may produce an acceptable result without acquiring the knowledge or judgment that should come from the process. In the arts, struggle, experimentation, failure, revision, and critique are not obstacles to learning. They are the learning. Our responsibility is to help students understand the difference between using a tool to extend their thinking and using it to replace their thinking.

ES: I know that working in academia can be both inspiring and draining. How do you recharge? LMT: I recharge by returning to the things that remind me I am more than my administrative role. I make artwork, I read constantly, and I love movies. Those activities allow me to move into a different mental space after days that can be filled with meetings, budgets, personnel issues, schedules, and decisions. I am also part of the Nuestra Artists Collective, which has been especially important to me. Being in community with other artists gives me the encouragement and accountability to continue making work while serving as a dean. Administration can consume every available hour if you let it, so maintaining a creative practice has to be intentional. The collective reconnects me to the part of myself that existed before I became an administrator and, in many ways, makes me better at the work I do now. ES: What career accomplishments are you most proud of? LMT: Earning my Ph.D. is one of the accomplishments of which I am most proud, not simply because of the degree itself, but because of what it represents in my family’s story. My parents had only an elementary-level education in Mexico, and I grew up without a roadmap for navigating higher education. To move from being the child of immigrants who did not know that studying photography in college was even an option, to earning an MFA and ultimately a doctorate, remains deeply significant to me. I am especially proud that my doctoral work allowed me to remain an artist. My Ph.D. in Aesthetic Studies included a creative dissertation that brought together scholarly writing and photographic practice and culminated in an exhibition. I did not have to choose between being a scholar and being a maker. The work I am sharing with Lenscratch readers comes from that project, so it represents both an academic accomplishment and an important chapter in my development as an artist.

ES: What is the most meaningful part of your job? LMT: The most meaningful part of my job is helping faculty succeed so that they, in turn, can help students succeed. I spent many years in the classroom, so I understand how much energy, preparation, creativity, and care good teaching requires. As a dean, I now have the opportunity to remove barriers, advocate for programs, solve problems, find resources, and create structures that allow faculty to concentrate on students and their disciplines. There is something deeply satisfying about work that may never have my name attached to it but makes someone else’s good work possible. I loved the direct connection I had with students as a professor. As a dean, the connection is more indirect, but the potential reach is much larger. When faculty feel supported and programs are healthy, students benefit. That is the part of administration that continues to feel purposeful to me.

ES: How do you see your photography evolving in the next few years?

LMT: I hope my photography evolves into something I do not fully recognize yet. That possibility is exciting to me. I have been making work around Mexican immigrant experience, family, culture, and identity since 1995, and those concerns are so deeply connected to who I am that I do not imagine they will disappear. But the visual language I use to explore them is changing.

I am becoming more interested in suggestion than description, and in images that operate poetically rather than documentarily. I want to explore what can be communicated through objects, fragments, spaces, cultural references, constructed images, and perhaps processes I have not used before. The shift away from photographing identifiable people is already pushing me to think differently about representation and about what it means to make work rooted in a community while also protecting the people within it.

After so many years of making photographs, I no longer feel that evolution has to mean abandoning what came before. It can mean allowing the same questions to take a different form. I want to remain curious enough to let the work surprise me. If, a few years from now, I can still recognize the concerns at the heart of the photographs but not necessarily the way I chose to express them, I will consider that a good place to be.

Lupita Murillo Tinnen was born in Fort Worth, Texas. She serves as Dean of Academic Affairs and Workforce at Collin College Plano Campus. Tinnen earned a Ph.D. in Aesthetic Studies at the University of Texas at Dallas. Her dissertation addressed the historical portrayal of immigrants in documentary photography, the use of the photograph for social advocacy, and defined methods for the post-documentary. She holds an MFA in Photography from the University of North Texas and a BA in Photography from East Texas A&M. Her work focuses on cultural and personal issues stemming from her background as a first-generation Mexican American. Additionally, Tinnen served on the Society for Photographic Educators board of directors (2012-2016, Treasurer, 2014-2016). She served on the Texas Photographic Society Board of Directors (2010, Treasurer, 2015-2018). She is a member of the ArtCentre of Plano Board, and a member of the Nuestra Artist Collective.

Name: The best reviewed film in history.

Age: Not even out yet, except in the US and Canada.

Appearance: Coming soon to a screen near you.

How exciting! What is it? It’s called You Can See Everything .

Who’s in it? DiCaprio ? De Niro ? Both? It’s not that kind of film.

What’s it about, then? The subject of the documentary is Elizabeth Holmes , the disgraced founder of …

Did you say documentary? No thanks. But reviews of this particular documentary have been overwhelmingly favourable!

I don’t go to the cinema to learn things. Critics have been unstinting in their praise for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s unflinching three-hour examination of the Theranos scandal’s architect and …

Three hours? Are you kidding? I know that seems long, but the Guardian’s critic called it “a stupefying and gloriously destabilising hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject”. And audiences have so far been undaunted by the long run time – it logged a phenomenal $15m at the box office in its opening weekend in the US and Canada.

Meh. And the film has earned an unprecedented Metacritic score of 99/100.

Unprecedented? Certainly for a documentary – in fact, you’d have to go back to the 2016 drama Moonlight to find a best picture Oscar-winner with the same score.

You mean it’s higher than The Odyssey ? The Odyssey got 88/100.

Bigger than Digger? Digger got 46 .

At the end of the day, Metacritic is just one review aggregator. On Rotten Tomatoes, You Can See Everything has a 99% rating from 117 reviews so far, putting it in contention for the site’s best-rated film of 2026. It’s also effectively the highest rated cinema release ever on Letterboxd.

Effectively ? With a 4.7/5 score, it’s the fourth-highest reviewed overall, but the three above it are a live Radiohead concert and two TV shows (Band of Brothers and Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood).

Where are some of the other highest-rated films in history? Metacritic’s top 10 best-rated films include Citizen Kane (1941), The Leopard (1963), The Conformist (1970) and Tokyo Story (1972).

Those movies all have one thing in common: I haven’t seen them. It’s early days, obviously, but You Can See Everything is already 24th on Metacritic’s all-time list.

What are some of the worst -rated films? Rotten Tomatoes’ bottom 10 (of films that have received 20 reviews or more) includes: Tom & Jerry: The Forbidden Compass (2025); Left Behind (2014), starring Nicolas Cage; Roberto Benigni’s adaptation of Pinocchio (2002); and Superbabies: Baby Geniuses 2 (2004), which Joanne Kaufman of the Wall Street Journal described as “unspeakably ghastly”.

Fortunately, I haven’t seen any of those either. I don’t know where you would even find them.

Do say: “The hype is deserved.”

Don’t say: “The nachos were excellent.”
